metadata.description: Scenario-Based Study Guide for GCP Professional Data Engineer certification - validates ability to design, build, operationalize, secure, and monitor data processing systems on Google Cloud.

questions.title: BigQuery Architecture Selection
questions.scenario: A media streaming company ingests 50TB of viewing analytics daily. Their analysts run ad-hoc queries joining viewing data with a 500GB user profile table. Queries need to return in under 30 seconds for interactive dashboards. Data is partitioned by date but analysts frequently query across 90-day windows. The monthly BigQuery cost is $200K, with 80% attributed to query scanning.
questions.questionText: Which BigQuery optimization strategy provides the greatest cost reduction while maintaining query performance?

choices.text: Cluster tables on frequently filtered columns (user_id, content_category), use materialized views for common 90-day aggregations, and implement BigQuery editions with autoscaling slots for predictable pricing
Move all data to BigQuery BI Engine for in-memory acceleration
Switch to on-demand pricing and let BigQuery automatically optimize
Export data to Cloud Storage and query with Dataproc Hive for lower cost

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Clustering reduces bytes scanned per query, materialized views pre-compute common aggregations, and slots provide predictable pricing at scale.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Clustering on user_id and content_category ensures queries filtering on these columns skip irrelevant data blocks — reducing scan volume by 80-95% for selective queries. Materialized views pre-compute 90-day aggregations that analysts query repeatedly — BigQuery automatically routes queries to materialized views when they satisfy the query pattern. BigQuery editions with autoscaling slots provide predictable cost (no per-TB scanning charges) while auto-scaling compute to meet the 30-second SLA. Combined, these address both cost (from per-TB to slots + reduced scans) and performance.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Clustering provides block-level pruning — BigQuery stores min/max metadata per block and skips non-matching blocks during scans.
  • Materialized views are automatically refreshed and BigQuery's optimizer rewrites queries to use them transparently.
  • BigQuery editions (Standard/Enterprise/Enterprise Plus) use slot-based pricing — predictable costs regardless of query volume.
  • Autoscaling: slots scale from baseline to max slots based on query demand — no over-provisioning during off-peak hours.

questions.title: Streaming Pipeline Design
questions.scenario: An IoT platform ingests 2 million sensor events per second from industrial equipment. Events must be: deduplicated (sensors may send duplicates within a 10-minute window), enriched with equipment metadata from a slowly-changing dimension table, aggregated in 1-minute tumbling windows for real-time dashboards, and written to BigQuery for historical analysis. Late-arriving data (up to 1 hour late) must be incorporated into the correct window.
questions.questionText: Which GCP architecture handles deduplication, enrichment, windowed aggregation, and late data?

choices.text: Pub/Sub to Cloud Functions for processing, Firestore for state, and scheduled BigQuery loads
Cloud IoT Core directly to BigQuery streaming API with deduplication at query time
Pub/Sub for ingestion, Dataflow (Apache Beam) for deduplication with state, side-input enrichment, windowed aggregation with allowed lateness, and BigQuery streaming insert for output
Kafka on GKE for ingestion and processing with custom Kubernetes pods for each processing stage

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Dataflow (Apache Beam) provides exactly-once processing with stateful deduplication, side inputs for enrichment, and windowing with late data handling.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Pub/Sub provides durable, scalable ingestion at millions of messages/second with at-least-once delivery. Dataflow (Apache Beam) handles: stateful deduplication using a dedup transform with a 10-minute state TTL, side-input enrichment from the metadata table (refreshed periodically), tumbling window aggregation with allowed lateness of 1 hour (late data updates the window result), and exactly-once BigQuery streaming output. Dataflow autoscales workers based on backlog and provides built-in monitoring. This is the canonical GCP streaming pipeline pattern.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Dataflow deduplication: use a stateful DoFn with a BagState keyed by event ID with a timer for TTL cleanup.
  • Side inputs: a periodically refreshed view of the metadata table joined with each event for enrichment.
  • Allowed lateness: window.withAllowedLateness(Duration.standardHours(1)) — late elements trigger window re-computation.
  • BigQuery Storage Write API (vs. legacy streaming): provides exactly-once semantics and higher throughput (no dedup at sink needed).

questions.title: Data Lake Storage Strategy
questions.scenario: A genomics research company stores 5PB of sequencing data. Access patterns vary dramatically: active research data (1%) is accessed hundreds of times daily, recent project data (10%) is accessed weekly, publication data (30%) is accessed yearly for audits, and archival data (59%) has not been accessed in 3 years but must be retained for 15 years. They want to minimize storage cost while maintaining access when needed.
questions.questionText: Which Cloud Storage configuration minimizes cost for these access patterns?

choices.text: Store everything in Standard class and rely on Autoclass to optimize automatically

Manually assign: Standard for active (1%), Nearline for recent (10%), Coldline for publication (30%), Archive for archival (59%), with Object Lifecycle Management rules transitioning objects based on age
All data in Archive class with restore-on-demand for any access
Use Autoclass with terminal storage class set to Archive for the entire bucket

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Autoclass automatically moves objects between storage classes based on actual access patterns — no manual lifecycle rules needed when patterns are unpredictable at the object level.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Autoclass monitors access patterns per object and automatically transitions between Standard, Nearline, Coldline, and Archive classes. With terminal class set to Archive, objects untouched for extended periods automatically reach the cheapest tier. Objects that are accessed get promoted back to faster tiers automatically. This is superior to manual lifecycle rules for genomics data where individual files' access patterns are hard to predict (a specific sequence file might be accessed unexpectedly for a new research project). No manual classification or lifecycle management needed — Autoclass handles the 5PB transparently.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Autoclass: per-object automatic tiering based on access. No minimum storage duration charges (unlike manual class assignment).
  • Autoclass management fee: $0.0025/1000 objects/month — minimal at genomics file sizes (GBs per file = fewer objects).
  • Terminal storage class setting determines the coldest tier Autoclass will use — Archive enables maximum savings.
  • Autoclass promotes objects back to Standard on access — subsequent reads are at Standard latency, not Archive retrieval delays.

questions.title: ML Pipeline Integration
questions.scenario: A retail company wants to build a product recommendation model. Training data (purchase history, browsing behavior, product catalog) lives in BigQuery (2TB). They need: feature engineering using SQL (familiar to their team), automated model retraining weekly, model versioning and A/B testing, and prediction serving at 10,000 requests per second with sub-100ms latency. The team has limited ML infrastructure experience.
questions.questionText: Which GCP ML architecture minimizes infrastructure management while meeting all requirements?

choices.text: Export data to GCS, train with custom TensorFlow on Vertex AI Training, deploy to Vertex AI Endpoints with traffic splitting

BigQuery ML for feature engineering and model training (SQL-based), export trained model to Vertex AI Model Registry, deploy to Vertex AI Endpoints with traffic splitting for A/B testing, and Cloud Scheduler triggering weekly retraining
Dataproc with Spark MLlib for training, deploy to GKE with TensorFlow Serving
AutoML Tables in Vertex AI with automatic feature engineering and deployment

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: BigQuery ML enables SQL-based training on data already in BigQuery, while Vertex AI handles deployment and A/B testing — minimal infrastructure.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: BigQuery ML allows the team to train models using SQL (CREATE MODEL ... AS SELECT) directly on their 2TB BigQuery data — no data export, no Python/TensorFlow expertise needed for the core training loop. Feature engineering uses familiar SQL transformations. The trained model exports to Vertex AI Model Registry for versioning. Vertex AI Endpoints provide autoscaling prediction serving (handles 10K RPS at sub-100ms) with traffic splitting for A/B testing between model versions. Cloud Scheduler triggers a weekly BigQuery ML training job and model promotion pipeline. This is the lowest-infrastructure-management path.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• BigQuery ML supports: linear/logistic regression, boosted trees, matrix factorization (recommendations), deep neural networks, and imported TensorFlow models.
  • Matrix factorization in BigQuery ML is purpose-built for recommendations: CREATE MODEL ... OPTIONS(model_type='matrix_factorization').
  • Vertex AI Endpoints auto-scale based on request rate and support canary deployments (1% new model, 99% current).
  • BigQuery ML TRANSFORM clause defines reproducible feature engineering applied at both training and prediction time.

questions.title: Data Governance Architecture
questions.scenario: A financial services company uses BigQuery as their enterprise data warehouse with 10,000 datasets across 50 projects. They need: automatic discovery and classification of PII (names, SSNs, account numbers), column-level access control preventing analysts from seeing PII in shared datasets, data lineage tracking from source through transformations to consumption, and a searchable data catalog so analysts can find relevant datasets without asking the data team.
questions.questionText: Which GCP services provide comprehensive data governance for this environment?

choices.text: Dataplex for data discovery and cataloging, Cloud DLP for automatic PII detection and classification, BigQuery column-level security with policy tags for access control, and Data Lineage API for tracking data flow through pipelines
BigQuery IAM roles at the dataset level with manual PII tagging by data owners
A custom-built data catalog application with manual data classification processes
Google Workspace Data Loss Prevention policies applied to BigQuery exports only

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Map each governance requirement to the purpose-built GCP service: discovery (Dataplex), classification (DLP), access control (policy tags), lineage (Data Lineage API).

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Dataplex provides automated data discovery across BigQuery and GCS, with a searchable catalog including business metadata and quality scores. Cloud DLP automatically scans datasets to detect and classify PII (100+ built-in info types including SSN, credit card, phone numbers). BigQuery column-level security with policy tags restricts column access: a "PII" policy tag applied to SSN/name columns prevents unauthorized users from querying those columns regardless of dataset-level permissions. Data Lineage API automatically captures lineage from BigQuery jobs, Dataflow pipelines, and Dataproc jobs — showing the complete transformation path from source to consumption.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Dataplex data quality: auto-profiling computes statistics (nulls, distinct counts, patterns) for catalog entries.
  • DLP integration with BigQuery: scan results can auto-apply policy tags to detected PII columns — zero manual classification.
  • Policy tags use IAM fine-grained reader roles: bigquery.dataPolicyReader role grants access to masked/unmasked data per tag.
  • Data Lineage API: automatic capture for BigQuery (CTAS, INSERT, MERGE), Dataflow, Dataproc, and Composer jobs.

questions.title: Batch Pipeline Orchestration
questions.scenario: A company runs 200 daily batch jobs with complex dependencies: some jobs depend on data from multiple upstream jobs completing, some jobs must run in a specific order within a group, and some groups can run in parallel. They need: dependency management, retry with exponential backoff, SLA monitoring (alert if pipeline doesn't complete by 6 AM), and the ability to backfill historical data by re-running specific date ranges. Currently using cron with manual dependency tracking.
questions.questionText: Which GCP service provides production-grade batch orchestration with all required capabilities?

choices.text: Cloud Scheduler triggering Cloud Functions in sequence
Cloud Composer (managed Apache Airflow) with DAGs defining dependencies, retry policies, SLA callbacks, and parameterized backfill runs via CLI
Pub/Sub messages triggering Cloud Functions for each job in the pipeline
Workflows (serverless orchestration) with step-level retries and conditions

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Apache Airflow (Cloud Composer) is purpose-built for complex DAG dependencies, SLA monitoring, retries, and backfill operations.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Cloud Composer (managed Airflow) defines pipelines as DAGs (Directed Acyclic Graphs) with explicit task dependencies — handling complex multi-dependency patterns naturally. Built-in features include: retry with configurable delay and exponential backoff, SLA miss callbacks that trigger alerts when tasks exceed time limits, and the ability to backfill specific date ranges via `airflow backfill --start-date --end-date`. For 200 daily jobs with complex interdependencies, Airflow's DAG model is the industry standard for batch orchestration. Workflows is simpler but lacks backfill capability and complex dependency modeling.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Cloud Composer 2: autoscaling environment with pay-per-use worker pricing and shared tenant infrastructure.
  • Airflow operators for GCP: BigQueryOperator, DataflowOperator, DataprocOperator, GCSOperator — native integration.
  • SLA monitoring: sla parameter on tasks triggers sla_miss_callback when execution exceeds the specified duration.
  • Backfill: `gcloud composer environments run ENVIRONMENT --location LOCATION dags backfill -- DAG_ID -s START -e END`.

questions.title: Change Data Capture Pipeline
questions.scenario: A company needs to replicate data from their on-premises PostgreSQL database (500 tables, 10TB) to BigQuery in near-real-time. They need: initial full load of all tables, ongoing CDC (change data capture) with sub-minute latency, schema evolution handling (new columns added to source should appear in BigQuery automatically), and minimal impact on the source database performance.
questions.questionText: Which GCP service provides managed CDC from PostgreSQL to BigQuery?

choices.text: Custom Debezium deployment on GKE writing to Pub/Sub, then Dataflow to BigQuery
Scheduled Data Transfer Service with full table extracts every 5 minutes
Datastream for PostgreSQL — managed CDC service with initial snapshot, continuous replication, schema evolution, and direct BigQuery destination
Cloud SQL PostgreSQL replica with federated queries from BigQuery

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Datastream is GCP's managed CDC service — handles initial load, continuous replication, and schema changes without custom infrastructure.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Datastream provides fully managed CDC from PostgreSQL (and MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server) to BigQuery or GCS. It performs: initial backfill (full snapshot of existing data), continuous change capture using PostgreSQL's logical replication (minimal source impact), automatic schema evolution (new columns in source are added to BigQuery destination), and delivers changes with sub-minute latency. No infrastructure to manage — Datastream handles connectivity, replication slot management, and destination writing. Direct BigQuery destination applies changes as streaming inserts with merge semantics.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Datastream uses PostgreSQL logical replication (pgoutput plugin) — reads WAL without impacting read/write performance.
  • Schema evolution: new columns detected automatically; dropped columns become nullable in destination.
  • BigQuery destination options: merge (apply updates/deletes) or append-only (write all changes as inserts for full history).
  • Connectivity: supports private connectivity (VPC peering, VPN, Interconnect) for on-premises sources via connection profiles.

questions.title: Bigtable Design for Time-Series
questions.scenario: A smart grid company stores power consumption readings from 10 million smart meters. Each meter reports every 15 seconds. They need: single-row lookups for the latest reading per meter (sub-10ms), range scans for a specific meter's readings over a time period, and aggregate queries across all meters in a geographic region for demand forecasting. Data retention is 2 years. Daily ingestion is 50 billion rows.
questions.questionText: Which Bigtable row key design supports all three access patterns efficiently?

choices.text: Row key: timestamp#meter_id — enables time-range scans across all meters
Row key: region#meter_id#timestamp — optimizes geographic queries but creates hotspots

Row key: meter_id#reverse_timestamp — enables latest reading lookup (first row per meter) and per-meter time range scans; separate table or column family with region#reverse_timestamp for geographic aggregations
Row key: random_hash#meter_id#timestamp — eliminates hotspots but prevents range scans

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Reverse timestamp ensures the most recent reading is the first row for a given meter prefix — enabling both latest-value lookup and historical range scans.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Row key meter_id#reverse_timestamp (where reverse_timestamp = Long.MAX_VALUE - timestamp): querying with row prefix "meter_123#" returns the latest reading first (lowest reverse_timestamp = most recent). Range scans for a meter's history use start/end row keys with the meter prefix and time bounds. For geographic aggregation, a secondary access pattern uses either: a separate table keyed by region#reverse_timestamp, or BigQuery federated queries over Bigtable for complex aggregations. The meter_id prefix distributes writes across Bigtable nodes (assuming meter IDs are reasonably distributed).

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Reverse timestamp: Long.MAX_VALUE - epoch_millis ensures lexicographic ordering returns newest first.
  • 10M meters writing every 15s = 666K writes/second — well within Bigtable's scaling capability (10K+ writes/node).
  • Column families: separate 'latest' (single cell, overwritten) from 'history' (versioned cells) for different access patterns.
  • Bigtable garbage collection policies: retain max 2 years of versions per cell for automatic data expiration.

questions.title: Real-Time Feature Store
questions.scenario: An e-commerce company serves ML predictions (fraud detection, recommendations) requiring features computed from both real-time events (last 5 minutes of user activity) and batch-computed features (lifetime purchase history, user segments). Feature computation must be consistent between training (batch) and serving (real-time). Features must be served at p99 latency under 20ms for 50,000 predictions per second.
questions.questionText: Which architecture provides consistent feature computation across batch and real-time with low-latency serving?

choices.text: Compute all features in BigQuery at prediction time using federated queries
Redis cluster on GKE with custom feature computation logic duplicated in training and serving code
Vertex AI Feature Store with batch features ingested from BigQuery and streaming features computed by Dataflow and ingested in real-time, served via online serving layer with sub-20ms lookups
Precompute all features hourly in BigQuery and cache in Memorystore for serving

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Vertex AI Feature Store bridges batch and streaming features with a unified online serving layer — ensuring training/serving consistency.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Vertex AI Feature Store provides: batch ingestion from BigQuery (lifetime features computed in scheduled queries), streaming ingestion from Dataflow (real-time features like 5-minute activity aggregations), and a low-latency online serving endpoint (sub-10ms lookups). Feature definitions are shared between training and serving — ensuring consistency (no training/serving skew). The same feature entity (user_id) can have both batch features (updated daily) and streaming features (updated in real-time) served together in a single lookup. Online serving is backed by optimized storage designed for high-throughput point lookups.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Feature Store online serving supports 50K+ QPS with sub-10ms p99 latency using Bigtable-backed storage.
  • Feature monitoring: automatic drift detection between training data distribution and serving-time feature values.
  • Point-in-time correct joins: Feature Store provides historical feature values at the exact timestamp of training labels.
  • Streaming ingestion: Dataflow writes features via the Feature Store Streaming Ingestion API with exactly-once semantics.

questions.title: Data Encryption and Access Control
questions.scenario: A healthcare company stores patient data in BigQuery. Regulatory requirements mandate: encryption at rest with customer-managed keys (CMEK), specific key per dataset for different data classifications, key rotation every 90 days, and column-level encryption for SSN and medical record numbers so that even BigQuery administrators cannot read those values without a separate decryption key.
questions.questionText: Which encryption architecture satisfies both CMEK and column-level encryption requirements?

choices.text: CMEK with Cloud KMS keys (one per dataset classification) for at-rest encryption with 90-day rotation, plus AEAD encryption functions (KEYS.NEW_KEYSET, AEAD.ENCRYPT) for SSN/MRN columns using a separate keyset that administrators cannot access
Default Google-managed encryption with column-level access control via policy tags
Client-side encryption of all data before loading into BigQuery
CMEK only with DLP to redact sensitive columns from query results

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: CMEK handles at-rest encryption at the table/dataset level; AEAD functions provide additional column-level encryption controlled by a separate key.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: CMEK with Cloud KMS provides customer-controlled encryption at rest — separate keys per dataset classification with configured 90-day automatic rotation. For column-level protection beyond what CMEK provides (since CMEK is transparent — authorized BigQuery users can still read decrypted data), AEAD encryption functions encrypt specific column values with a keyset stored in Cloud KMS. Only users with access to the specific AEAD keyset can decrypt those columns. BigQuery administrators without KMS access to the AEAD key see only ciphertext in SSN/MRN columns. This provides defense-in-depth: CMEK for infrastructure encryption + AEAD for application-level column encryption.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• CMEK in BigQuery: specified at table creation, encrypts data, temporary files, and metadata with the customer's KMS key.
  • AEAD functions: AEAD.ENCRYPT(keyset, plaintext, additional_data) — deterministic or non-deterministic encryption options.
  • Key rotation for CMEK: Cloud KMS automatic rotation creates new key version every 90 days; old versions retained for decryption.
  • Separation of duties: KMS admin (manages keys) vs. BigQuery admin (manages data) — neither alone can access encrypted column values.

questions.title: Multi-Cloud Data Architecture
questions.scenario: A company stores 100TB in AWS S3 and 50TB in Azure Blob Storage. They chose BigQuery as their unified analytics platform. They need to query data across all three clouds without moving the data permanently (data residency requirements keep data in its original cloud). Queries must join GCP-native BigQuery tables with S3 and Azure data.
questions.questionText: Which BigQuery feature enables cross-cloud querying without permanent data movement?

choices.text: Use Data Transfer Service to copy all data into BigQuery on a schedule
BigQuery Omni with cross-cloud connections — run BigQuery SQL on data in S3 and Azure Blob Storage in-place, join results with GCP-native tables
Create external tables pointing to S3 and Azure using federated queries
Set up Datastream CDC from AWS and Azure databases into BigQuery

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: BigQuery Omni extends BigQuery's compute to AWS and Azure regions — querying data where it lives without moving it.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: BigQuery Omni deploys BigQuery compute nodes in AWS and Azure regions (running on Anthos). You create external connections to S3 buckets and Azure Blob containers, then query using standard BigQuery SQL. Data stays in its original cloud (satisfying data residency). Cross-cloud joins work by moving only the query results (small intermediate results) between clouds — bulk data never moves. This provides a unified SQL interface across all three clouds while respecting data locality requirements.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• BigQuery Omni supports: AWS (us-east-1, eu-west-1, etc.) and Azure (eastus2, westeurope, etc.) regions.
  • Cross-cloud transfers: only aggregated/filtered results cross cloud boundaries — minimizing egress costs.
  • External tables on Omni support: Parquet, ORC, Avro, CSV, and JSON formats in S3/Blob Storage.
  • Limitations: Omni tables are read-only; DML operations require data in GCP-native BigQuery tables.

questions.title: Dataproc Serverless vs Provisioned
questions.scenario: A company runs three types of Spark workloads: daily ETL jobs (4 hours, predictable resource needs, cost-sensitive), ad-hoc data exploration by analysts (unpredictable timing, 15-minute average sessions), and weekly ML training (8 hours, GPU-intensive, requires specific library versions). They currently run everything on a single always-on Dataproc cluster costing $15K/month with 60% average utilization.
questions.questionText: Which Dataproc configuration optimizes cost and flexibility for these three workload types?

choices.text: Keep the single always-on cluster and optimize utilization with YARN scheduling
Migrate everything to Dataflow for unified serverless processing
Three separate always-on clusters — one per workload type

Dataproc Serverless for ad-hoc exploration (instant startup, no cluster management), scheduled ephemeral cluster for daily ETL (created, runs, deleted — pays only for execution time), and a specialized GPU cluster with custom image for weekly ML training (created on schedule, deleted after)

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Match each workload's characteristics to the right Dataproc mode: serverless for ad-hoc, ephemeral for scheduled batch, specialized for GPU training.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Dataproc Serverless provides instant Spark sessions for analysts — no cluster startup wait, no idle cost between sessions, scales automatically. For daily ETL, an ephemeral cluster (created via workflow template, runs the job, auto-deletes) pays only for the 4 execution hours — no idle cost. For ML training, a purpose-built cluster with GPU nodes (A100/T4) and a custom image (pre-installed libraries) spins up weekly, trains for 8 hours, and deletes. This eliminates the $15K/month always-on cost, paying only for actual compute time across all three patterns.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Dataproc Serverless: Spark sessions start in seconds, auto-scale workers, no cluster configuration — billed per DCU-hour used.
  • Ephemeral clusters via workflow templates: `gcloud dataproc workflow-templates` define cluster + job as a single unit.
  • Custom images: pre-installed Python packages, CUDA drivers, and configuration — eliminates initialization actions overhead.
  • Cost comparison: always-on at 60% util = paying for 40% idle; ephemeral/serverless = 0% idle cost.

questions.title: Database Selection for Operational Data
questions.scenario: A gaming company needs a database for their player profile service. Requirements: global availability (players in 30+ countries), sub-5ms read latency, strong consistency for in-game purchases (cannot double-spend virtual currency), automatic horizontal scaling to handle 100K read and 10K write operations per second, and the ability to run complex queries joining player profiles with inventory and achievements tables.
questions.questionText: Which GCP database meets all requirements for global, strongly consistent, relational operations at this scale?

choices.text: Cloud Firestore in Native mode for global availability and auto-scaling
Cloud Spanner — globally distributed, strongly consistent relational database with horizontal scaling, SQL support, and sub-5ms reads from local replicas
Cloud SQL PostgreSQL with read replicas in each region
Bigtable for low-latency reads with application-level consistency enforcement

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Cloud Spanner is the only GCP database providing global distribution + strong consistency + relational SQL + horizontal scaling simultaneously.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Cloud Spanner provides: global distribution across 30+ countries with multi-region configurations, strong consistency (external consistency — the strongest form) preventing double-spend issues, automatic horizontal scaling handling 100K+ reads and 10K+ writes/second, full SQL support with joins across tables (player profiles JOIN inventory JOIN achievements), and sub-5ms reads from the nearest replica using stale reads (bounded staleness of a few seconds is acceptable for profiles). For purchases requiring strong consistency, Spanner's TrueTime-based transactions guarantee no double-spending.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Spanner multi-region configs: nam6 (US), eur6 (Europe), nam-eur-asia1 (global) — data replicated across continents.
  • Stale reads (bounded_staleness: 5s) provide sub-5ms local reads without cross-region round-trips.
  • Strong reads for purchases: cross-region Paxos commit ensures consistency at the cost of higher latency (100-200ms for cross-continent).
  • Auto-scaling: Spanner provisions compute nodes automatically with managed autoscaler (based on CPU or storage thresholds).

questions.title: BigQuery Analytics Patterns
questions.scenario: A marketing analytics team runs repetitive queries: daily cohort analysis (same query structure, different date parameters), real-time campaign dashboards (same 10 queries refreshed every 5 minutes), and monthly reports joining 5 large tables (2TB+ scan each time). They spend $50K/month on BigQuery compute. The team wants to reduce cost and improve query response time for dashboards without changing their SQL queries.
questions.questionText: Which BigQuery features reduce both cost and latency for these query patterns?

choices.text: Increase slot reservations to run queries faster
Schedule all queries during off-peak hours for lower pricing
Cache all query results in Memorystore for application-level caching

Materialized views for the daily cohort patterns (auto-maintained), BI Engine reservation for dashboard queries (in-memory acceleration), and partitioning/clustering on the large tables to reduce scan volume for monthly reports

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Match each query pattern to its optimizer: materialized views for repetitive structures, BI Engine for dashboards, partitioning for large scans.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Materialized views pre-compute the cohort analysis pattern — BigQuery automatically serves queries from the materialized view when the query matches its definition (no SQL changes needed). BI Engine provides an in-memory acceleration layer for the 10 dashboard queries — sub-second response for repeated queries on the same data. Partitioning by date and clustering on join keys for the monthly report tables reduces 2TB scans to only the relevant partitions (potentially 90%+ reduction). Together these address all three patterns: repetitive structure (MVs), repeated exact queries (BI Engine), and large scans (partition pruning).

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Materialized views: BigQuery optimizer automatically rewrites matching queries to use the MV — transparent to users.
  • BI Engine: in-memory analysis service with sub-second response; allocated per project (1GB to 250GB reservation).
  • MV auto-refresh: BigQuery maintains MVs automatically when base tables are modified — always consistent.
  • Cost impact: MVs eliminate redundant computation (same query daily = computed once); BI Engine = fixed cost vs. per-query scanning.

questions.title: VPC Service Controls
questions.scenario: A government agency uses BigQuery and Cloud Storage for classified data analysis. Requirements: no data can be exfiltrated from the project (even by authorized users with IAM permissions), API calls to BigQuery and GCS must only originate from within the agency's VPC network (not from the public internet), and data cannot be copied to external projects or buckets even using authorized service accounts.
questions.questionText: Which security configuration prevents data exfiltration while allowing authorized internal access?

choices.text: IAM permissions restricting users from creating export jobs or storage transfers
Cloud Armor rules blocking API requests from external IP addresses
Organization policies restricting resource creation to specific projects

VPC Service Controls perimeter around the project — restricting BigQuery and GCS APIs to only accept requests from the internal VPC, with ingress/egress rules blocking data movement to external projects

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: VPC Service Controls create a security perimeter that prevents data from leaving defined boundaries — even with valid IAM credentials.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: VPC Service Controls define a security perimeter around GCP projects. Services inside the perimeter (BigQuery, GCS) reject API calls from outside the perimeter (public internet, other projects) — even with valid IAM credentials. Egress rules block data from being copied, exported, or streamed to resources outside the perimeter. This prevents: BigQuery result export to external GCS buckets, GCS object copies to external projects, and API access from non-VPC networks. The perimeter operates at the network and project level — complementing IAM (which only controls identity-based access).

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• VPC-SC perimeter restricts at the API level: even `gsutil cp` with owner permissions fails if crossing the perimeter boundary.
  • Access levels: combine VPC network origin, IP ranges, device policies, and identity attributes for fine-grained ingress rules.
  • Bridge perimeters: allow controlled data sharing between specific perimeters without opening to the world.
  • Dry-run mode: test perimeter configurations without enforcing — audit logs show what would be blocked.

questions.title: Hybrid Data Processing
questions.scenario: A manufacturing company has on-premises Hadoop clusters processing factory sensor data (HDFS, Hive, Spark jobs). They want to gradually migrate to GCP but cannot move all data immediately due to latency requirements for real-time factory control systems. During migration (18 months), they need to run analytics across both on-premises HDFS data and GCP-resident data in BigQuery, using existing Hive queries and Spark jobs with minimal rewriting.
questions.questionText: Which hybrid architecture enables gradual migration with cross-environment analytics?

choices.text: Full lift-and-shift of all Hadoop workloads to Dataproc immediately
Keep all analytics on-premises and use GCS only for cold archival storage
Run BigQuery federated queries directly against on-premises HDFS

Dataproc with Cloud Storage as the primary data lake, HDFS connector for on-premises data access, BigQuery connector for Spark jobs needing BigQuery data, and Hive metastore shared between on-premises and Dataproc for unified table discovery

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Dataproc runs the same Spark/Hive workloads as Hadoop but can access both Cloud Storage and on-premises HDFS simultaneously during migration.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Dataproc runs Apache Spark and Hive with minimal code changes from existing Hadoop jobs. During migration: GCS replaces HDFS as the primary storage (using gs:// paths), the HDFS connector enables reading on-premises data over the network (via Cloud Interconnect/VPN), and the BigQuery connector allows Spark to read/write BigQuery tables directly. A shared Hive metastore (or Dataproc Metastore service) provides unified table discovery across both locations — analysts see tables from both environments in the same catalog. Jobs migrate incrementally as data moves from HDFS to GCS.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Dataproc Metastore: managed Hive Metastore service shared across multiple Dataproc clusters and accessible from on-premises.
  • Cloud Storage connector (gcs-connector): drops into existing Spark/Hive jobs — change hdfs:// to gs:// in paths.
  • BigQuery connector for Spark: spark.read.format("bigquery").load("project.dataset.table") — reads BigQuery as a DataFrame.
  • Cloud Interconnect provides low-latency, high-bandwidth connectivity for HDFS access during the 18-month transition.

questions.title: Pub/Sub Message Ordering
questions.scenario: A financial trading platform publishes order events (placed, filled, cancelled) to Pub/Sub. Downstream consumers must process events for the same order in sequence (cannot process a cancellation before the placement). Events for different orders can be processed in parallel. The system handles 500,000 events per second with occasional 2x spikes. Some consumers are slower than others and may fall behind temporarily.
questions.questionText: Which Pub/Sub configuration ensures per-order event ordering while maintaining high throughput?

choices.text: Single Pub/Sub topic with a single subscriber — processes all messages sequentially
Multiple topics — one per order — with individual subscribers
Pub/Sub with ordering keys set to order_id — guarantees per-key message ordering while allowing parallel processing across different orders, with flow control for slow consumers
Pub/Sub Lite for lower cost with custom ordering logic in the application

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Pub/Sub ordering keys guarantee in-order delivery for messages with the same key while allowing parallelism across different keys.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Pub/Sub ordering keys (set to order_id) guarantee that messages with the same key are delivered to subscribers in publication order. Messages with different keys (different orders) are delivered in parallel — maintaining high throughput across 500K events/second. If a subscriber fails to acknowledge a message with ordering key X, subsequent messages with key X are held until acknowledgment (preserving order), while messages with other keys continue flowing. Flow control settings (max_outstanding_messages, max_outstanding_bytes) prevent slow consumers from being overwhelmed during 2x spikes.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Ordering keys: published with publish_time ordering guarantee per key; subscribers receive in order per key.
  • Ordering + parallelism: 500K events with 100K unique order_ids = 5 events/order on average, all orders process in parallel.
  • Flow control: subscriber StreamingPullRequest sets max_outstanding limits to prevent memory exhaustion during spikes.
  • Exactly-once delivery: combine ordering keys with Pub/Sub exactly-once delivery feature (subscription-level) for financial correctness.

questions.title: BigQuery Storage Optimization
questions.scenario: A company's BigQuery bill shows $80K/month in storage costs for 2PB of data. Analysis reveals: 40% of tables haven't been queried in 6 months, 30% of tables have time-partitioned data where only the most recent 90 days are ever queried, 20% are staging tables that should be deleted after pipeline completion, and 10% are active analytics tables. They want to reduce storage cost by 60% without losing data.
questions.questionText: Which combination of BigQuery storage features achieves the 60% cost reduction?

choices.text: Export all data to Cloud Storage in Parquet format and delete from BigQuery
Compress all tables using BigQuery's built-in compression and accept query performance degradation

Enable long-term storage pricing (automatic for tables not modified in 90 days), set partition expiration on time-partitioned tables to drop partitions older than 90 days, implement pipeline cleanup for staging tables, and use table clones instead of copies for active tables
Move all rarely-accessed tables to a cheaper BigQuery edition

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Long-term storage is 50% cheaper (automatic), partition expiration drops unneeded data, and cleanup of staging tables eliminates waste.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Long-term storage pricing automatically applies to tables not modified for 90+ consecutive days — 50% cheaper ($0.01/GB vs $0.02/GB for active storage). This covers the 40% unqueried tables immediately (querying does not affect the classification — only modifications do). Partition expiration drops partitions beyond 90 days for the 30% where only recent data is queried — eliminating 80%+ of those tables' storage. Staging table cleanup (DROP TABLE in pipeline completion steps) eliminates the 20% waste. Combined: 40% at 50% discount + 30% mostly deleted + 20% deleted = well over 60% total reduction.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Long-term storage: automatic — any table/partition unmodified for 90 days transitions without action needed.
  • Partition expiration: ALTER TABLE SET OPTIONS(partition_expiration_days=90) — partitions older than 90 days auto-deleted.
  • Table clones: zero-cost copy that shares storage with the base table — only differences consume additional storage.
  • Time travel storage: BigQuery retains 7 days of change history — this counts toward storage costs and can be reduced to 2 days minimum.

questions.title: Streaming Analytics with Dataflow
questions.scenario: A ride-sharing company processes trip events in real-time: trip_started, location_updates (every 5 seconds), trip_completed, and payment_processed. They need to compute: average trip duration per city (5-minute windows), surge pricing zones (1-minute sliding windows of demand), and end-of-trip billing that must wait for the payment_processed event before finalizing (session windowing). Each computation has different latency requirements: surge pricing must update within 10 seconds, billing can wait up to 5 minutes.
questions.questionText: Which Dataflow windowing strategy handles all three computations with their different latency needs?

choices.text: Single global window with periodic triggers for all computations
Three separate Dataflow pipelines — one per computation — each with a single window type
Only fixed windows at 1-minute intervals for all computations

Multiple windowing strategies in the same pipeline: fixed 5-minute windows for trip duration, sliding 1-minute windows with 10-second triggers for surge pricing, and session windows (gap-based) with payment event as session end for billing

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Apache Beam supports multiple window types in the same pipeline — apply different windows to different PCollections based on computation requirements.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: A single Dataflow pipeline branches the input PCollection into three paths: (1) Trip duration uses FixedWindows(5 minutes) with AfterWatermark trigger — 5-minute aggregation per city. (2) Surge pricing uses SlidingWindows(1 minute, sliding every 10 seconds) with early triggers every 10 seconds — providing continuous demand calculation. (3) Billing uses Sessions(gap=5 minutes) — groups all events for a trip until no new events arrive for 5 minutes (or payment_processed arrives), then computes the final bill. Different triggers on each window control latency: surge fires every 10 seconds, billing fires on session close.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Sliding windows: Window.into(SlidingWindows.of(Duration.standardMinutes(1)).every(Duration.standardSeconds(10))).
  • Session windows: events are grouped by key (trip_id) with a gap duration — no events for gap_duration closes the session.
  • Triggers: AfterProcessingTime(10s) fires speculative results for surge; AfterWatermark fires final results for billing.
  • Single pipeline advantage: shared Pub/Sub subscription, single autoscaling pool, and consistent processing of related events.

questions.title: Data Loss Prevention Pipeline
questions.scenario: A company ingests customer support chat transcripts into BigQuery for sentiment analysis. Customers sometimes share sensitive information (credit card numbers, SSNs, email addresses, phone numbers) in chat messages. The company must: detect PII before data reaches the analytics team, de-identify PII (replace with tokens that preserve format for analytics), maintain a secure mapping for re-identification by authorized compliance staff only, and produce audit reports showing what was de-identified.
questions.questionText: Which GCP service and configuration provides detection, de-identification, secure re-identification, and auditing?

choices.text: Regular expressions in a Dataflow pipeline to detect and replace PII patterns
BigQuery column-level security to hide PII columns from the analytics team

Cloud DLP (Sensitive Data Protection) with inspection for PII detection, format-preserving encryption (FPE) for de-identification using a wrapped KMS key, Cloud DLP re-identification API accessible only to compliance role, and Cloud Audit Logs for tracking all de-identification operations
Client-side masking before data ingestion using application-level string replacement

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Cloud DLP provides detection (100+ info types), de-identification (FPE preserves format), and re-identification (controlled by KMS key access).

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Cloud DLP (now called Sensitive Data Protection) provides: inspection jobs that detect 100+ PII types (credit cards, SSNs, emails, phone numbers) in text data, format-preserving encryption (FPE) using CryptoReplaceFfxFpeConfig which replaces PII with tokens of the same format (a credit card number becomes another 16-digit number — preserving analytics on format/length without exposing real data). The encryption key is wrapped with Cloud KMS — only users with KMS decrypt permission can re-identify. Cloud Audit Logs capture every DLP operation with who/what/when for compliance. This pipeline runs in Dataflow or as DLP jobs before data reaches BigQuery.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• FPE (Format-Preserving Encryption): deterministic — same input produces same token, enabling JOIN/GROUP BY on tokenized values.
  • DLP inspection: configurable likelihood threshold (VERY_LIKELY, LIKELY, POSSIBLE) controls sensitivity vs. false positives.
  • Re-identification: DLP reidentify API requires both the wrapped key AND KMS decrypt permission — separation of duties.
  • DLP job triggers: can run on data in GCS, BigQuery, or Datastore; results stored in BigQuery for audit reporting.

questions.title: Data Mesh Architecture on GCP
questions.scenario: A large enterprise has 20 business domains (marketing, finance, supply chain, etc.) each with their own data products. They want to implement data mesh principles: domain ownership of data, self-serve data infrastructure, federated governance, and data as a product with SLAs. Each domain team should independently manage their data pipelines and publish datasets for cross-domain consumption without centralized bottlenecks.
questions.questionText: Which GCP architecture implements data mesh with domain independence and federated governance?

choices.text: Single BigQuery project with datasets per domain and centralized data engineering team managing all pipelines
A central data lake in GCS with domain-specific folders and a single orchestration layer

Domain-owned GCP projects with their own BigQuery datasets and pipelines, Dataplex for federated discovery and governance across domains, Analytics Hub for publishing data products with access controls and SLA metadata, and shared taxonomy for consistent data classification
Separate GCP organizations per domain with no cross-domain data sharing capability

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Data mesh on GCP: domain projects for ownership, Dataplex for governance, Analytics Hub for data product publishing — federated but discoverable.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Each domain owns a GCP project with their BigQuery datasets, Cloud Composer/Dataflow pipelines, and IAM boundaries — full autonomy for data production. Dataplex provides federated governance: a central catalog discovering data assets across all domain projects, applying consistent data quality rules and classification without centralizing control. Analytics Hub allows domains to publish curated data products (shared datasets) with descriptions, SLA commitments, and access request workflows — consumers subscribe without data copying. A shared taxonomy (policy tags, data classes) ensures consistent PII handling across domains while each domain enforces independently.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Analytics Hub: publishers create listings (BigQuery datasets), subscribers get linked datasets — shared in place, no copying, always fresh.
  • Dataplex lakes and zones: organize assets from multiple projects into logical domains for unified governance.
  • Dataplex data quality: define rules centrally, execute in each domain's project — results visible in the central catalog.
  • Data mesh principles: domain ownership (separate projects), data as product (Analytics Hub listings with SLAs), self-serve platform (Dataplex + standard tools), federated governance (shared taxonomy + Dataplex).

questions.title: Data Fusion Pipeline Development
questions.scenario: A company's data integration team manages 100 data sources (databases, SaaS applications, files, APIs) that feed into BigQuery. The team includes data engineers comfortable with code and business analysts who need to build simple integrations without coding. They need: a visual pipeline builder for non-developers, reusable transformation plugins for common patterns (address parsing, phone normalization), preview capability before running full pipelines, and lineage tracking across all integrations.
questions.questionText: Which GCP service provides visual pipeline building with code-free and code-based options for diverse teams?

choices.text: Cloud Data Fusion — visual pipeline designer with 200+ pre-built connectors, custom plugin support for reusable transforms, data preview mode, and built-in lineage tracking across all pipelines
Dataflow with Apache Beam SDK only — engineers write Java/Python code for all pipelines
Dataproc with Hive scripts for ETL, run on a shared cluster
BigQuery stored procedures for all data transformation with scheduled queries

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Cloud Data Fusion is a visual ETL/ELT tool with a drag-and-drop interface, plugin ecosystem, and built-in governance features.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Cloud Data Fusion provides a visual, code-free pipeline designer (CDAP-based) where business analysts drag and drop connectors and transforms. It includes 200+ pre-built connectors (databases, SaaS apps, file systems), supports custom plugins (Java-based reusable components for address parsing, phone normalization, etc.), offers data preview mode (run transforms on sample data before full execution), and automatically tracks data lineage across all pipeline runs. Engineers can also write custom plugins or use the Wrangler (interactive data preparation) for complex transformations. Pipelines execute on Dataproc clusters under the hood for scalability.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Data Fusion editions: Basic (visual pipelines), Enterprise (adds replication, lineage, metadata, and Wrangler).
  • Plugin Hub: community and custom plugins installable from a marketplace — extend connectivity and transformation capabilities.
  • Wrangler: interactive data preparation with 100+ directives (parse, split, format, merge) applied step-by-step with instant preview.
  • Lineage: field-level lineage tracking showing which source fields map to which destination fields through all transformation steps.

questions.title: Data Warehouse Modernization
questions.scenario: A company migrating from Teradata to BigQuery has 500 tables with complex stored procedures, macros, and BTEQ scripts. The Teradata system uses specific SQL dialects (QUALIFY, SAMPLE, temporal tables) not directly available in standard SQL. They need to migrate both the data and the SQL workload with minimal rewriting while maintaining query result consistency.
questions.questionText: Which migration approach minimizes manual SQL rewriting from Teradata to BigQuery?

choices.text: Manually rewrite all SQL to BigQuery Standard SQL — hire consultants for the 500 tables
Export all data to CSV and load into BigQuery without migrating any SQL logic
Keep Teradata running alongside BigQuery and migrate one table at a time over 3 years

BigQuery Migration Service with automated SQL translation (Teradata to BigQuery SQL), batch SQL translator for stored procedures and scripts, interactive SQL translator for ad-hoc queries, and validation mode comparing results between source and target

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: BigQuery Migration Service includes automated SQL translation that converts Teradata SQL dialect to BigQuery SQL with high accuracy.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: BigQuery Migration Service provides: automated SQL translation from Teradata (and other sources) to BigQuery SQL — handling dialect differences like QUALIFY (converted to window function subqueries), SAMPLE (converted to TABLESAMPLE), and temporal tables. The batch translator processes entire codebases of stored procedures and BTEQ scripts. The interactive translator allows analysts to paste individual queries and see the translated result. Validation mode runs queries on both systems and compares results to ensure correctness. This dramatically reduces manual rewriting — typical translation rates are 80-90% automatic with manual intervention only for complex edge cases.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• SQL Translation Service supports: Teradata, Hive, Spark SQL, Redshift, Oracle, SQL Server, Netezza, and Presto dialects.
  • QUALIFY in Teradata becomes a subquery with ROW_NUMBER() in BigQuery (BigQuery also added native QUALIFY support recently).
  • Batch translation API: submit entire .sql files or directories, receive translated output with confidence scores per statement.
  • Data migration: BigQuery Data Transfer Service supports direct Teradata transfer (extracts, transfers, and loads automatically).

questions.title: Vertex AI AutoML vs Custom Training
questions.scenario: A company needs to build two ML models: (1) a document classification model for 50 categories with 100K labeled training documents, and (2) a custom fraud detection model requiring specialized feature engineering, ensemble methods, and real-time scoring with model explainability. The data science team has 2 PhD-level ML engineers and 5 data analysts who know SQL but not Python.
questions.questionText: Which training approach is appropriate for each model given team skills and requirements?

choices.text: AutoML for both models to minimize engineering effort

AutoML Natural Language for document classification (analysts can manage), custom training on Vertex AI with XGBoost ensemble for fraud detection (ML engineers develop), both deployed to Vertex AI Endpoints with Explainable AI enabled
Custom training for both models using TensorFlow on Vertex AI Training
BigQuery ML for both models since the team knows SQL

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Match model complexity to team skills: AutoML for the straightforward classification (non-coder friendly), custom training for the specialized fraud model (requires ML expertise).

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: AutoML Natural Language for document classification: upload labeled data, AutoML handles architecture selection, hyperparameter tuning, and training — no ML expertise needed, analysts can manage the lifecycle. For fraud detection: custom training on Vertex AI enables the ML engineers to implement specialized feature engineering, ensemble methods (XGBoost + neural network + rules), and custom loss functions optimized for fraud detection's asymmetric cost structure. Both models deploy to Vertex AI Endpoints. Explainable AI provides feature attributions for fraud decisions (regulatory requirement for explaining why a transaction was flagged).

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• AutoML NL: achieves competitive accuracy for classification tasks with 1,000+ examples per category — 100K total is excellent.
  • Custom training: containerized training jobs with any framework (XGBoost, TensorFlow, PyTorch, scikit-learn) on Vertex AI Training.
  • Explainable AI: feature-based explanations (which features contributed most to this prediction) — critical for fraud model transparency.
  • Cost efficiency: AutoML charges per training hour with no infrastructure management; custom training charges per compute unit used.

questions.title: IAM Best Practices for Data Teams
questions.scenario: A data platform serves 200 users across roles: data engineers (pipeline development), data scientists (model training with GPU access), analysts (query and visualization), and data stewards (governance and access management). The current setup gives all users the BigQuery Admin role at the project level. The security team demands least-privilege access while maintaining team productivity and self-service capabilities.
questions.questionText: Which IAM strategy implements least privilege for these four data roles?

choices.text: Create custom roles for each persona with exactly the permissions needed, use IAM conditions to restrict access to specific datasets/resources, and implement attribute-based access with resource tags for team-specific resources
Keep BigQuery Admin for everyone but add VPC Service Controls to prevent data exfiltration
Use predefined roles: BigQuery Data Editor for all users, with an admin escalation process for special operations
Separate projects per role with full admin in each project

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Custom roles with IAM conditions provide exact permissions per persona without over-provisioning — the gold standard for least privilege.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Custom roles define exact permissions: Data Engineers get bigquery.jobs.create, bigquery.tables.create/update/delete, dataflow.jobs.create — but not bigquery.datasets.setIamPolicy. Data Scientists get Vertex AI training permissions and GPU quota but not production data write access. Analysts get bigquery.jobs.create and bigquery.tables.getData but not table creation/modification. Data Stewards get bigquery.datasets.setIamPolicy and dlp.inspectContent but not data querying. IAM conditions restrict further: resource.name matches specific datasets, or request.time within business hours. Tags enable team-specific resource isolation without separate projects.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Custom roles: up to 300 permissions, scoped to project or organization level, versionable and testable.
  • IAM conditions: resource.name, resource.type, request.time — enable row-level IAM without policy proliferation.
  • Recommender API: analyzes actual permission usage over 90 days and suggests permission removals for over-privileged roles.
  • Policy Analyzer: answers "who can access resource X" across the entire organization — essential for security audits.

questions.title: Event-Driven Architecture
questions.scenario: A company needs to build a data pipeline triggered by events: when a new file lands in Cloud Storage, process it within 5 minutes; when a BigQuery table is updated, refresh downstream materialized views; when a Pub/Sub dead-letter queue receives messages, alert the operations team and create a ticket. They want minimal always-on infrastructure and pay-per-execution pricing.
questions.questionText: Which GCP event-driven architecture handles all three trigger patterns with minimal infrastructure?

choices.text: Eventarc routing Cloud Storage events, BigQuery audit logs, and Pub/Sub messages to Cloud Run services (or Cloud Functions) for serverless event-driven processing
Cloud Scheduler polling each resource every minute to detect changes
Always-on Compute Engine instances monitoring each event source with custom scripts
Cloud Composer DAGs with sensors for each event source

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Eventarc provides a unified eventing layer that routes events from GCP services to serverless compute — no polling, no always-on infrastructure.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Eventarc is GCP's unified event routing service. It captures: Cloud Storage object creation events (via Cloud Audit Logs or direct integration), BigQuery job completion events (via audit logs), and Pub/Sub message delivery failures. These events are routed to Cloud Run services or Cloud Functions 2nd gen for processing — serverless, pay-per-invocation, scales to zero. For GCS: object finalize event triggers a Cloud Run job that processes the file. For BigQuery: tabledata.insertAll audit log triggers a function that refreshes materialized views. For DLQ: Pub/Sub push subscription triggers an alerting function. No always-on compute needed.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Eventarc triggers: Cloud Audit Logs (90+ GCP services), direct events (GCS, Pub/Sub), and third-party events (via Eventarc for third-party).
  • Cloud Run Jobs: for batch processing triggered by events — run to completion, no need for HTTP endpoint.
  • Exactly-once processing: Eventarc provides at-least-once delivery; combine with idempotent handlers for exactly-once semantics.
  • Event filtering: Eventarc routing supports filters on event attributes (e.g., only trigger on specific bucket or table names).

questions.title: Data Transfer at Scale
questions.scenario: A company needs to migrate 500TB of historical analytics data from their on-premises data warehouse to BigQuery. Their internet bandwidth is 1 Gbps (shared with production traffic). At 1 Gbps, the transfer would take 46 days. They have a 4-week migration window. The data is in CSV and Parquet formats stored on NAS storage. After the initial migration, they need ongoing daily incremental transfers of 2TB.
questions.questionText: Which migration approach meets the 4-week timeline for initial load and handles ongoing incremental transfers?

choices.text: gsutil rsync over the 1 Gbps internet connection with parallel composite uploads
Transfer Appliance (physical device) for the initial 500TB bulk load, followed by Storage Transfer Service with scheduled daily incremental transfers over the network for the ongoing 2TB
Set up a dedicated 10 Gbps Cloud Interconnect and transfer everything over the network
BigQuery Data Transfer Service with scheduled loads from on-premises via a local agent

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: 500TB in 4 weeks over shared 1 Gbps is impossible — physical transfer (Transfer Appliance) solves the initial load, then network handles daily 2TB increments.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Google Transfer Appliance is a physical device (100TB or 300TB capacity) shipped to the customer's site. Data is copied to the appliance locally (at NAS speed, not internet speed), then shipped to Google for ingestion into Cloud Storage. For 500TB, two 300TB appliances (shipped in parallel) can complete the transfer within the 4-week window including shipping time. After migration, the daily 2TB incremental uses Storage Transfer Service over the 1 Gbps connection (2TB at 1 Gbps = ~4.5 hours — well within the daily window). Data loads from GCS to BigQuery using BigQuery load jobs.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Transfer Appliance: 100TB (TA100) and 300TB (TA480) models. Turnaround time: ~2 weeks (ship + copy + ship + ingest).
  • Data on appliance is encrypted with customer-managed keys — secure in transit.
  • Storage Transfer Service: managed file transfer with scheduling, bandwidth throttling, and integrity verification.
  • BigQuery load jobs from GCS: free (no charge for batch loads); supports CSV, Parquet, ORC, Avro, and JSON.

questions.title: Choosing Between Firestore and Bigtable
questions.scenario: A company builds two services: (1) a mobile app backend storing user profiles, preferences, and activity feeds with complex queries (filter by multiple fields, order by timestamp, paginate) for 10 million users at 50K reads/second, and (2) a telemetry service storing device metrics at 1 million writes/second with single-key lookups and time-range scans only (no complex queries). Both need sub-10ms latency.
questions.questionText: Which database assignment optimizes for each workload's access patterns?

choices.text: Bigtable for both workloads due to higher throughput capability
Firestore (Native mode) for the mobile app backend (complex queries, indexing, real-time listeners), Bigtable for the telemetry service (single-key lookups, range scans, 1M writes/second throughput)
Firestore for both workloads due to simpler developer experience
Cloud SQL for the mobile app and Cloud Spanner for the telemetry service

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Firestore excels at complex queries with automatic indexing; Bigtable excels at massive throughput with simple access patterns.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Firestore Native mode provides: composite indexes enabling multi-field queries (filter by region AND status, order by timestamp), real-time listeners for mobile app activity feeds, pagination via query cursors, and offline sync for mobile. It handles 50K reads/second with automatic scaling. Bigtable provides: single-digit millisecond latency at 1M+ writes/second, row-key prefix scans for time-range queries, and linear horizontal scaling by adding nodes. Bigtable cannot do complex queries (no secondary indexes, no multi-field filters) — but the telemetry service doesn't need them. Each service gets the database optimized for its access pattern.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Firestore: auto-scaling, serverless pricing (per read/write/storage), composite indexes, real-time listeners, offline support.
  • Bigtable: manual scaling (add/remove nodes), fixed-capacity pricing, single row key design, no automatic indexing.
  • Throughput: Firestore scales to ~10K writes/second per database; Bigtable scales to 10K+ writes/second per node (add nodes linearly).
  • Decision matrix: complex queries = Firestore/Spanner; simple high-throughput = Bigtable; ACID transactions = Spanner/Firestore.

questions.title: BigQuery Scheduled Queries and Procedures
questions.scenario: A data warehouse team maintains 50 daily transformation jobs: fact table loads depend on dimension table loads completing first, some queries use MERGE statements for SCD Type 2 updates, error handling must retry failed steps without re-running successful ones, and the entire DAG must complete by 6 AM for business reporting. Currently using bash scripts calling bq CLI sequentially.
questions.questionText: Which approach provides dependency management, error handling, and scheduling for BigQuery transformations?

choices.text: BigQuery scheduled queries running independently with no dependency management
Dataform for all transformations with dependency resolution and scheduling
Cloud Functions triggered on a timer calling BigQuery jobs sequentially
BigQuery stored procedures called from Cloud Composer (Airflow) DAGs with task dependencies, retry logic, SLA miss alerts, and conditional execution based on upstream task success

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Dataform (now integrated in BigQuery) is purpose-built for SQL-based transformation DAGs with dependencies, scheduling, and error handling.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Dataform (integrated into BigQuery Studio) provides: SQL-based transformation definitions with explicit dependencies (ref() function for table references), automatic DAG construction from dependencies, built-in scheduling with SLA configuration, incremental processing support for MERGE/SCD operations, assertions (data quality checks that halt downstream processing on failure), and unit testing. It is purpose-built for the exact scenario described — SQL transformations with dependencies and scheduling. For 50 transformation jobs that are all BigQuery SQL, Dataform is more appropriate than Cloud Composer (which adds Airflow infrastructure overhead for a SQL-only workload).

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Dataform SQLX: extends SQL with ref(), config(), and incremental() blocks for dependency and incremental processing.
  • ref() function: SELECT * FROM ${ref("dim_customers")} — creates automatic dependency and resolves table references.
  • Assertions: SELECT * FROM table WHERE condition — if rows returned, the assertion fails and downstream tables are not built.
  • Dataform vs Composer: Dataform for SQL-only transformations in BigQuery; Composer for multi-system orchestration (GCS + Dataflow + BigQuery + external APIs).

questions.title: Cross-Project Data Sharing
questions.scenario: A company has a central data warehouse project containing curated datasets. Five business unit projects need read access to specific datasets — not all datasets. The data team wants: no data copying between projects (single source of truth), per-dataset access granularity (marketing sees marketing datasets, finance sees finance datasets), query costs charged to the consuming project (not the data warehouse project), and the ability to revoke access instantly if a project is decommissioned.
questions.questionText: Which BigQuery data sharing approach satisfies all requirements?

choices.text: Grant each project's service account BigQuery Data Viewer role at the project level on the data warehouse
Authorized views in each consuming project querying the source datasets
Dataset-level IAM grants for each business unit's user group, with cross-project querying (consuming project is billed for compute), and IAM condition-based access that can be revoked per dataset
Analytics Hub with published listings per dataset and subscriber access per business unit

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Dataset-level IAM provides per-dataset granularity, cross-project queries bill the querying project, and IAM revocation is instant.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Dataset-level IAM: grant bigquery.dataViewer role to each business unit's Google Group on specific datasets only — marketing group gets marketing dataset access, finance group gets finance datasets. When users query from their own project (SELECT * FROM `data-warehouse-project.marketing_dataset.table`), BigQuery bills compute to the querying project (not the data warehouse). No data is copied — queries read directly from the source. Revocation is instant: remove the IAM binding and access is immediately denied. This provides exactly the per-dataset granularity, cost attribution, and instant revocation required.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Cross-project billing: BigQuery charges the project where the query job runs (the user's project) for compute, not the data project.
  • Dataset-level roles: bigquery.dataViewer (read), bigquery.dataEditor (read+write), bigquery.dataOwner (full control).
  • Google Groups for IAM: add/remove users from groups without touching IAM policies — simplifies user lifecycle management.
  • Alternative: Analytics Hub provides additional features (listings marketplace, linked datasets, audit) for more formalized data sharing programs.

questions.title: Cost-Effective Analytics Architecture
questions.scenario: A startup processes 10TB of data daily on a tight budget ($5K/month). Workloads include: nightly batch ETL (transform raw logs into analytics tables), hourly aggregation jobs (compute metrics), weekly ML model retraining, and ad-hoc analyst queries during business hours. They currently use a dedicated Dataproc cluster running 24/7 for all workloads at $8K/month.
questions.questionText: Which architecture reduces costs below $5K/month while handling all workload types?

choices.text: Keep the Dataproc cluster but downsize to smaller instances
Move everything to Cloud Functions for pay-per-invocation pricing

Replace Dataproc with: BigQuery for ETL and aggregation (SQL-based, on-demand pricing), BigQuery ML for model training (eliminates separate compute), and BigQuery with BI Engine reservation for analyst queries — all serverless, pay only for processing
Use Compute Engine preemptible instances for all processing

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: BigQuery's on-demand pricing (pay per query) eliminates idle compute cost — ideal for a startup with varied workload timing.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Replacing the always-on Dataproc cluster with BigQuery eliminates $8K of fixed infrastructure: ETL transforms run as BigQuery scheduled queries (SQL-based, charged per TB scanned). Hourly aggregations use the same scheduled query mechanism. BigQuery ML trains models using SQL without separate GPU instances. Analyst queries use on-demand pricing during business hours only. With 10TB daily ingestion and assuming columnar format with partitioning, actual scan volume per query is much less than 10TB. On-demand BigQuery at $6.25/TB scanned, combined with storage optimization (long-term pricing, partition expiration), easily fits within $5K/month with no idle cost.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• BigQuery free tier: 1TB/month of queries + 10GB/month storage — covers initial exploration at zero cost.
  • Cost optimization levers: partitioning (scan only relevant dates), clustering (skip irrelevant blocks), and column pruning (SELECT only needed columns).
  • BigQuery ML training: costs are compute charges during training — typically $5-50 per training run depending on data size.
  • Migration path: convert Spark/PySpark transformations to BigQuery SQL — most aggregation and transformation logic translates directly.

questions.title: Schema Registry and Evolution
questions.scenario: A company publishes events from 50 microservices through Pub/Sub topics. Each service evolves its event schema independently. Consumers need to: know the schema of messages they receive, handle backward-compatible changes (new optional fields) without breaking, detect and reject breaking changes (field removal, type changes) before they reach production, and maintain a registry of all event schemas with version history.
questions.questionText: Which GCP approach manages schema evolution for Pub/Sub message contracts?

choices.text: Pub/Sub schema validation with schemas defined in Avro or Protocol Buffers, schema registry storing versions, topic-level schema enforcement rejecting non-conforming messages, and compatibility checks (backward, forward) on schema updates
Document schemas in a wiki and rely on developers to follow conventions
Use JSON for all messages with no schema enforcement — consumers handle whatever they receive
Embed the full schema in every message as a header field

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Pub/Sub has built-in schema support — schemas stored in a registry, enforced at the topic level, with compatibility checking for evolution.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Pub/Sub schema registry stores schemas (Avro or Protocol Buffers) with version history. Topics are associated with schemas — messages that don't conform to the schema are rejected at publish time (preventing bad data from entering the system). Schema revisions support compatibility modes: BACKWARD (new schema can read old messages — safe for consumers), FORWARD (old schema can read new messages — safe for producers). This prevents breaking changes from reaching production. Consumers use the registered schema to deserialize messages reliably, and the version history shows the full evolution of each event type.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Pub/Sub schema types: AVRO and PROTOCOL_BUFFER — both support rich type systems and evolution rules.
  • Schema validation: publisher receives an error if message doesn't match — fail-fast at source, not at consumer.
  • Compatibility checks: validate new schema version against previous before committing — block breaking changes proactively.
  • Protocol Buffers advantage: field numbers ensure wire compatibility; Avro advantage: schema embedded in data files for self-describing storage.

questions.title: BigQuery Materialized Views vs Tables
questions.scenario: A dashboard queries the same complex aggregation every 5 minutes: sales totals by region, product category, and day for the last 30 days from a 5TB fact table. The query scans 500GB each time and takes 45 seconds. The underlying data updates continuously (streaming inserts). The team wants sub-second dashboard response while always showing the latest data. Monthly query cost for this single dashboard is $20K.
questions.questionText: Which optimization provides sub-second response with fresh data and reduced cost?

choices.text: BigQuery materialized view on the aggregation query — automatically maintained on streaming inserts, serves queries from the pre-computed result, with BI Engine reservation for in-memory sub-second response
Pre-aggregate into a separate table refreshed every 5 minutes by a scheduled query
Cache the query result in application memory and refresh every 5 minutes
Create a BigQuery view (logical, not materialized) to simplify the query syntax
