hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Materialized views are auto-refreshed on data changes and serve queries from pre-computed results — no 500GB scan each time.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: BigQuery materialized views pre-compute and store the aggregation result. When the base table receives streaming inserts, BigQuery automatically updates the materialized view incrementally (only processing new data, not rescanning 500GB). Queries matching the materialized view pattern are served directly from the MV — near-zero bytes scanned, sub-second response. Adding BI Engine reservation caches the MV result in memory for truly instant response. Cost reduction: MV maintenance cost (incremental) is a fraction of repeated 500GB scans. The $20K/month drops to ~$500/month for MV maintenance plus BI Engine reservation.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• MV auto-refresh: after streaming inserts, MV is updated within minutes; query optimizer uses MV + delta from streaming buffer for fresh results.
  • MV cost: charged for the incremental maintenance query (much smaller than full 500GB scan) and storage of the aggregated result.
  • BI Engine: 1-250GB in-memory reservation; MV results cached for sub-100ms response on dashboards.
  • MV limitations: supports GROUP BY aggregations, INNER JOINs, and filtering — covers most dashboard query patterns.

questions.title: Data Quality Monitoring
questions.scenario: A data warehouse team needs to ensure data quality across 200 BigQuery tables. Requirements: detect anomalies (sudden volume drops, unexpected nulls, distribution shifts), validate business rules (referential integrity, value ranges, uniqueness constraints), run checks automatically after each pipeline execution, and produce a data quality scorecard visible to business stakeholders.
questions.questionText: Which GCP service provides automated data quality monitoring with anomaly detection and reporting?

choices.text: Custom SQL queries run after each pipeline with manual alerting on failures

Dataplex data quality rules — define expectations (completeness, accuracy, freshness, volume, uniqueness), auto-run after pipeline completion, anomaly detection on trends, and quality scores visible in Dataplex UI and exportable to dashboards
Great Expectations deployed on Compute Engine with custom scheduling
Cloud Monitoring with custom metrics for each quality dimension

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Dataplex data quality provides managed, declarative quality rules with automatic execution and scoring — integrated into the GCP data governance layer.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Dataplex data quality allows defining rules (YAML or UI) for: completeness (null checks), accuracy (value range, format), freshness (last update timestamp), volume (row count expectations), and uniqueness (duplicate detection). Rules run automatically after data updates (triggered by Dataplex or Cloud Composer) and produce quality scores (0-100%) per table and per rule dimension. Anomaly detection identifies sudden changes in quality metrics. Results are visible in the Dataplex UI, exportable to BigQuery for custom dashboards, and can trigger alerts via Cloud Monitoring. This provides the full observability loop without custom infrastructure.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Dataplex DQ rules: YAML definitions support SQL expressions for complex business rule validation.
  • Auto-discovery: Dataplex can suggest quality rules based on data profiling (inferred ranges, patterns, relationships).
  • Integration: Dataplex DQ results feed into data catalog entries — users see quality scores when discovering datasets.
  • Cost: DQ rules execute as BigQuery jobs — charged per bytes scanned, making it cost-effective compared to custom solutions.

questions.title: Disaster Recovery for Analytics
questions.scenario: A company's BigQuery-based analytics platform is critical for daily business operations. They need DR for: BigQuery datasets (50TB across 500 tables), Cloud Composer DAGs and configurations, Dataflow templates and pipeline definitions, and all associated IAM policies and service accounts. RPO is 4 hours and RTO is 2 hours. Primary region is us-central1 and DR region is us-east4.
questions.questionText: Which DR strategy meets the 4-hour RPO and 2-hour RTO for the full analytics platform?

choices.text: BigQuery cross-region dataset copies run manually when disaster is declared
Multi-region BigQuery dataset locations (US or EU) which automatically handle regional failures

BigQuery cross-region dataset replication (scheduled every 4 hours), Composer environment configuration in Git (re-deployable to any region), Dataflow Flex Templates stored in multi-regional GCS, and IAM policies exported via Terraform state in GCS with versioning
Rely on Google's internal replication for all services without additional configuration

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Each component needs its own DR mechanism: BQ cross-region replication for data, Git for configs, multi-regional GCS for templates, Terraform for IAM.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: BigQuery dataset cross-region replication (scheduled copy every 4 hours) ensures data availability in us-east4 within the 4-hour RPO. Cloud Composer DAGs and configuration stored in Git can be redeployed to a new Composer environment in us-east4 within minutes. Dataflow Flex Templates stored in multi-regional GCS (US) are accessible from any US region without action. IAM policies, service accounts, and org-level configurations managed via Terraform (state in GCS with versioning) can be re-applied to the DR region within the 2-hour RTO. This covers all four components with appropriate mechanisms per component type.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• BigQuery cross-region copy: BigQuery Data Transfer Service supports scheduled dataset copies between regions.
  • Multi-region BigQuery datasets (location: US) span multiple regions automatically — but cannot control which specific regions.
  • Composer DR: environment recreation from Git-stored DAGs takes 15-30 minutes; variable/connection state needs separate backup.
  • RTO optimization: pre-provision a scaled-down Composer environment in DR region (warm standby) for faster recovery.

questions.title: Lakehouse Architecture on GCP
questions.scenario: A company wants to build a lakehouse on GCP combining the flexibility of a data lake (schema-on-read, multi-format support, ML workloads) with data warehouse capabilities (ACID transactions, SQL analytics, BI tool integration). They store data in Cloud Storage in Delta Lake format and need: transactional consistency for concurrent readers and writers, time travel for auditing, and the ability to query from both BigQuery (SQL analytics) and Dataproc (Spark ML workloads).
questions.questionText: Which GCP lakehouse architecture provides ACID transactions, SQL analytics, and Spark access on shared data?

choices.text: BigLake tables over Delta Lake data in Cloud Storage — providing BigQuery SQL access with fine-grained security, Dataproc Spark access to the same Delta files with full ACID support, and unified metadata managed by BigLake Metastore
Cloud Storage with Parquet files and separate BigQuery external tables and Dataproc cluster
Copy data into BigQuery native tables for SQL and maintain a separate copy in GCS for Spark
Use BigQuery Storage API for all access, eliminating Cloud Storage

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: BigLake provides a unified access layer over open-format data (Delta, Iceberg) accessible from both BigQuery and Spark with consistent security.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: BigLake creates managed tables over Delta Lake (or Apache Iceberg) data in Cloud Storage. BigQuery queries BigLake tables via SQL with full performance optimization (predicate pushdown, column pruning). Dataproc Spark jobs read/write the same Delta files with full ACID transaction support (concurrent readers and writers, time travel). BigLake Metastore provides unified metadata — both BigQuery and Spark see the same tables and partitions. Fine-grained security (row and column-level) applied in BigLake is enforced regardless of which engine accesses the data. No data copying — single source of truth.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• BigLake supports: Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and Apache Hudi table formats on Cloud Storage.
  • BigLake Metastore: centralized metadata service compatible with both BigQuery and open-source tools (Spark, Presto).
  • Performance: BigQuery reads BigLake tables with native performance — storage API acceleration, no external table overhead.
  • Security: BigLake column-level security enforced for all access paths — prevents bypassing security by using Spark directly on GCS.

questions.title: Exactly-Once Processing Guarantees
questions.scenario: A payment processing pipeline must guarantee exactly-once processing: each payment event must be processed exactly once — no duplicates (would double-charge customers) and no missed events (would lose revenue). The pipeline reads from Pub/Sub, enriches with customer data, applies fraud rules, and writes to Cloud Spanner (for transaction records) and BigQuery (for analytics). Failures can occur at any stage.
questions.questionText: Which pipeline design guarantees exactly-once end-to-end processing across both sinks?

choices.text: Pub/Sub with ack/nack handling and application-level idempotency keys in each downstream write
Pub/Sub to Cloud Functions with retry enabled — functions are idempotent by design

Dataflow with exactly-once processing enabled, Pub/Sub exactly-once delivery subscription, idempotent writes to Spanner using transaction IDs, and BigQuery Storage Write API with exactly-once semantics
Kafka on GKE with exactly-once producer and consumer configurations

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Exactly-once requires: exactly-once source (Pub/Sub subscription), exactly-once processing (Dataflow), and exactly-once sinks (idempotent Spanner + BQ Storage Write API).

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: End-to-end exactly-once requires guarantees at every stage: Pub/Sub exactly-once delivery subscription deduplicates messages at the source. Dataflow's exactly-once processing ensures each element is processed once even across worker failures (using checkpointing and record deduplication). Spanner writes use transaction IDs as idempotency keys — reprocessed events produce the same transaction (no double-charge). BigQuery Storage Write API in exactly-once mode (committed streams) deduplicates based on offset — reprocessed writes are ignored. This chain guarantees no duplicates and no losses across both Spanner and BigQuery sinks.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Pub/Sub exactly-once: subscription-level dedup using message_id within the dedup window (configurable, default 10 minutes).
  • Dataflow checkpointing: runners checkpoint after bundles; on failure, replay from last checkpoint with fusion-aware dedup.
  • Spanner idempotent writes: INSERT OR UPDATE with transaction_id ensures replayed writes don't create duplicates.
  • BQ Storage Write API: committed streams track write offsets — duplicate appends at the same offset are safely ignored.

questions.title: Data Lifecycle Management
questions.scenario: A company stores 1PB of data in BigQuery with the following lifecycle: raw data (7-day retention, high query frequency), transformed data (90-day retention, moderate query frequency), aggregated analytics (2-year retention, weekly query frequency), and compliance archives (7-year retention, accessed only for audits). They want automated lifecycle management without manual intervention as data ages.
questions.questionText: Which BigQuery features automate the data lifecycle across all four stages?

choices.text: Time-partitioned tables with partition expiration per layer (7 days for raw, 90 days for transformed), scheduled query to aggregate before expiration, BigQuery long-term storage pricing for archives, and table expiration for compliance data after 7 years
Manual DBA intervention to delete expired data quarterly
Export all data to Cloud Storage and use Object Lifecycle Management exclusively
Keep all data in BigQuery indefinitely and rely on long-term pricing for cost management

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Partition expiration auto-deletes old partitions, long-term pricing auto-reduces cost for stable data, and table expiration handles compliance cleanup.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Partition expiration: raw tables set to 7 days auto-delete partitions older than 7 days (no manual cleanup). Before expiration, a scheduled query aggregates raw data into the transformed layer. Transformed tables set to 90 days similarly expire, with aggregation feeding the analytics layer before deletion. Analytics tables (2 years) automatically get long-term pricing after 90 days of no modification — 50% cheaper storage. Compliance archives use table expiration (DEFAULT_TABLE_EXPIRATION_DAYS = 2555 at dataset level) for automatic deletion after 7 years. This fully automated lifecycle requires zero manual intervention while handling all four stages with appropriate retention and cost optimization.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Partition expiration: ALTER TABLE SET OPTIONS(partition_expiration_days=7) — partitions older than 7 days auto-purge daily.
  • Long-term storage: tables/partitions not modified for 90 days automatically priced at $0.01/GB/month (vs $0.02 active).
  • Table expiration: set at table or dataset level — entire table deleted when age exceeds the threshold.
  • Pattern: raw(7d) → transform(90d) → aggregate(2y) → archive(7y) — each layer captures needed fidelity while upstream expires.

questions.title: Generative AI on Structured Data
questions.scenario: A company wants to enable business users to ask natural language questions about their BigQuery data warehouse. Users should be able to ask "What were our top 5 products by revenue last quarter in EMEA?" and get an answer without writing SQL. The system must: understand the company's specific schema and business terminology, respect existing access controls (users only see data they're authorized for), and handle ambiguous questions by asking for clarification.
questions.questionText: Which GCP capability enables natural language querying of BigQuery data with schema awareness and access control?

choices.text: Custom fine-tuned LLM trained on the company's SQL query history
Looker with natural language search over pre-built dashboards only
BigQuery natural language (Gemini in BigQuery) — schema-aware SQL generation from natural language, respecting IAM-based access control, with Duet AI clarification for ambiguous queries
Vertex AI custom text-to-SQL model deployed as an endpoint

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Gemini in BigQuery generates SQL from natural language using the actual schema context — and respects existing IAM permissions on the data.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Gemini in BigQuery (Duet AI for BigQuery) provides natural language to SQL translation that is schema-aware: it reads the table schemas, column descriptions, and metadata in the current project. When a user asks a question, Gemini generates the appropriate SQL query against their accessible tables — BigQuery executes it with the user's IAM context (respecting row-level and column-level security). For ambiguous questions (e.g., "revenue" could mean gross or net), it asks clarifying questions. Business glossary and column descriptions in the metadata improve accuracy for company-specific terminology. Users see both the natural language answer and the generated SQL for transparency.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Gemini in BigQuery uses table/column descriptions to understand domain-specific terminology — maintain good metadata for accuracy.
  • Generated queries run with the user's credentials — BigQuery IAM, column-level security, and RLS all apply as normal.
  • SQL generation is transparent: users see the generated SQL and can modify it — not a black box.
  • Supports complex queries: JOINs, aggregations, window functions, CTEs — not limited to simple SELECT statements.

questions.title: Audit and Compliance Logging
questions.scenario: A regulated financial company needs comprehensive audit logging for their GCP data platform. Requirements: log all BigQuery data access (who queried what data and when), log all IAM permission changes, retain logs for 7 years (regulatory requirement), detect anomalous access patterns (user querying unusual datasets at unusual hours), and produce monthly compliance reports showing all access to sensitive datasets.
questions.questionText: Which logging architecture provides comprehensive auditing with long-term retention and anomaly detection?

choices.text: Cloud Audit Logs (admin and data access) routed to BigQuery for long-term retention and analysis, Cloud Logging alert policies for anomaly detection, and scheduled BigQuery queries producing monthly compliance reports
Application-level logging in each service with custom log collection
Cloud Audit Logs with default 30-day retention and manual quarterly exports
Third-party SIEM ingesting all GCP logs with 7-year retention

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Cloud Audit Logs capture all data access; routing to BigQuery enables both 7-year retention and SQL-based compliance reporting.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Cloud Audit Logs automatically capture: Admin Activity (IAM changes, resource creation — always enabled, free) and Data Access logs (BigQuery queries, GCS reads — must be enabled). Log sink routes these to BigQuery for long-term retention beyond the default 30 days — BigQuery storage costs are minimal for log data and retention can be managed with partition expiration at 7 years. Alert policies on Cloud Logging detect anomalies (unusual query patterns, off-hours access, excessive data scans). Scheduled BigQuery queries over the audit log tables produce monthly compliance reports: "all users who accessed dataset X, with query text and timestamp."

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• BigQuery Data Access logs include: query text, tables accessed, bytes scanned, user identity, and client IP.
  • Log sink to BigQuery: creates partitioned tables (by day) — efficient for time-bounded compliance queries.
  • Anomaly detection: log-based metrics + Cloud Monitoring alerting policies trigger on unusual patterns.
  • Cost: Data Access logs can be voluminous — use exclusion filters to reduce cost for non-sensitive datasets while keeping full logging for sensitive ones.

questions.title: Data Pipeline Testing Strategy
questions.scenario: A data engineering team maintains 50 Dataflow pipelines and 100 BigQuery transformations. They experience: production failures from untested schema changes, data quality regressions caught by business users (not automated tests), difficulty testing pipelines locally before deployment, and no way to validate that a pipeline change produces the same output as the previous version. They want to adopt testing practices from software engineering.
questions.questionText: Which testing strategy provides comprehensive pipeline quality assurance?

choices.text: Run all pipelines in production and have business users validate outputs manually
Code review only — no automated testing infrastructure
Only test in staging environment with full production data copies

Unit tests for individual transforms (using DirectRunner for Beam), integration tests with test datasets in a dedicated project, data quality assertions in Dataform/BigQuery scheduled queries, and regression tests comparing new pipeline output against golden datasets

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Layered testing: unit tests for logic, integration tests for connectivity, assertions for quality, regression tests for correctness — same principles as software engineering.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Layered testing strategy: Unit tests use DirectRunner (local Beam runner) to test individual transforms with mock data — fast, no infrastructure needed. Integration tests run pipelines end-to-end in a dedicated test GCP project with synthetic test datasets, validating connectivity and schema handling. Data quality assertions (Dataform assertions or BigQuery checks) validate business rules in production (null checks, referential integrity, range validation) — catching regressions before business users. Regression tests compare new pipeline output against approved "golden" datasets — detecting unexpected changes in output when pipeline code is modified.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• DirectRunner: local Beam execution for unit tests — no Dataflow cluster needed, runs in seconds, supports all transforms.
  • Test project pattern: identical schema to production, synthetic data (no PII), used by CI/CD for integration validation.
  • Golden dataset comparison: hash or diff outputs against known-good results — regression detection for unintended behavior changes.
  • CI/CD integration: Cloud Build triggers tests on pull request, blocks merge if any layer fails — shift-left quality.

questions.title: IoT Data Ingestion at Scale
questions.scenario: A smart city project collects data from 500,000 sensors (traffic, air quality, noise, temperature) across 100 city blocks. Sensors send readings every 30 seconds. Total ingestion rate is 16,000 messages per second. They need: per-device authentication and management (firmware updates, configuration), message routing based on sensor type (traffic data to one pipeline, air quality to another), offline buffering (sensors should queue data during network outages), and a gateway pattern for sensors that cannot communicate directly with the cloud.
questions.questionText: Which GCP architecture handles half a million IoT devices with the specified management and routing requirements?

choices.text: Direct Pub/Sub publishing from each sensor over HTTP
Load balancer fronting Compute Engine instances running a custom MQTT broker
Cloud Functions HTTP endpoints per sensor type with API keys for authentication

IoT Core (or equivalent MQTT broker on GKE) for device authentication and management, with MQTT topics routing messages by sensor type to separate Pub/Sub topics, edge gateways (Cloud IoT Edge or Greengrass equivalent) for offline buffering and local aggregation from sensors that cannot reach the cloud directly

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: IoT device management requires: per-device auth (certificates), MQTT protocol, message routing, offline capability, and gateway patterns for constrained devices.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: An MQTT broker (self-managed on GKE since IoT Core was deprecated, or using a managed alternative like HiveMQ/EMQX on GKE) provides: per-device X.509 certificate authentication, MQTT protocol for low-bandwidth sensors, and topic-based message routing (traffic/# routes to traffic Pub/Sub topic, airquality/# to another). Edge gateways deployed at each city block aggregate data from nearby sensors (Bluetooth/Zigbee/LoRa devices that cannot speak MQTT directly), buffer during network outages, and forward when connectivity resumes. This architecture handles 500K devices with proper authentication, routing, and resilience.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Post-IoT Core: EMQX or HiveMQ on GKE provides MQTT 3.1.1/5.0 with Pub/Sub integration and per-device auth.
  • Edge gateways: run lightweight containers on local hardware; buffer messages in local storage during outages.
  • MQTT QoS levels: QoS 1 (at-least-once) for sensor data ensures no readings are lost during network instability.
  • Device management: OTA firmware updates pushed via MQTT control topics to individual devices or device groups.

questions.title: BigQuery Slots and Pricing Models
questions.scenario: A company runs three BigQuery workload types: (1) predictable daily ETL consuming 500 slot-hours per day, (2) interactive analyst queries varying from 100 to 2000 slot-hours per day unpredictably, and (3) monthly reporting consuming 5000 slot-hours over 2 days. Their current on-demand pricing costs $100K/month. They want to reduce cost while ensuring ETL always completes on time and analysts never wait more than 30 seconds for query results.
questions.questionText: Which BigQuery editions pricing configuration optimizes cost while meeting SLA requirements?

choices.text: Enterprise edition with a single autoscaling reservation for all workloads
Stay on on-demand pricing and add caching to reduce query frequency
Standard edition with maximum autoscaling for all workloads combined

Enterprise edition with: baseline reservation of 500 slots for ETL (guaranteed, predictable), autoscaling reservation (100-2000 slots) for analysts with max concurrency targets, and separate autoscaling reservation for monthly reporting jobs — each with appropriate priority levels

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Separate reservations with different baseline/autoscaling configs per workload type ensures SLAs while optimizing cost for each pattern.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Multiple reservations provide workload isolation: ETL reservation with 500 baseline slots (committed, cheapest per-slot pricing, guaranteed availability) ensures daily jobs always complete on time. Analyst reservation with 100 baseline + autoscaling to 2000 handles the variable query load — scales up during peak, scales down during quiet periods, maintaining the 30-second response SLA. Monthly reporting gets a separate autoscaling reservation that bursts high during the 2-day window and drops to zero otherwise. Priority levels (INTERACTIVE vs BATCH) within reservations ensure analyst queries preempt background jobs when slots are contended.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• BigQuery editions slots: baseline (committed, cheapest), autoscaling (on-demand rate, scale to zero when idle).
  • Reservation assignments: bind specific projects, folders, or organization to reservations for workload routing.
  • Priority: INTERACTIVE queries (analyst) preempt BATCH (ETL) within shared reservations — configurable per assignment.
  • Cost savings: committed baseline at annual rate is ~50-70% cheaper than on-demand equivalent; autoscaling pays only when used.

questions.title: Looker and Semantic Layer
questions.scenario: A company has 500 business users creating reports from BigQuery. Problems: different teams calculate "revenue" differently (some include returns, some don't), metrics definitions are embedded in individual reports (not reusable), and multiple conflicting dashboards create confusion about which numbers are "official". They need a single source of truth for business metrics with governed definitions that all reports use consistently.
questions.questionText: Which GCP solution provides a governed semantic layer with consistent metric definitions across all analytics?

choices.text: BigQuery views standardizing all metric calculations
Power BI connected to BigQuery with shared datasets per department

Looker with LookML modeling layer — centrally governed metric definitions (measures, dimensions, explore relationships) that all reports and dashboards reference, ensuring "revenue" means the same thing everywhere regardless of who builds the report
Google Sheets connected to BigQuery with named ranges for each metric formula

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Looker's LookML semantic layer defines metrics once centrally — all downstream reports inherit the governed definition automatically.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Looker's LookML (Looker Modeling Language) provides a semantic layer between BigQuery and business users. Metric definitions (like "revenue = SUM(amount) WHERE status != 'returned'") are defined once in LookML by data analysts or engineers. All reports, dashboards, and explorations built by 500 business users reference these governed definitions — they cannot accidentally calculate revenue differently. LookML models define dimensions, measures, relationships between tables (Explores), and access controls. Version-controlled in Git, reviewed via PR, and promoted through environments — the same governance as code. This eliminates conflicting metric definitions across departments.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• LookML is version-controlled in Git — metric definition changes go through code review before reaching production.
  • Derived tables: complex transformations defined in LookML, materialized in BigQuery as needed (PDTs — Persistent Derived Tables).
  • Looker universal semantic layer: Looker's semantic model can also serve metrics to other tools (Sheets, external apps) via Looker API.
  • Content validation: Looker validates all content (dashboards, looks) against the current LookML model — broken reports detected at deploy time.

questions.title: Data Masking and Tokenization
questions.scenario: A data team needs to provide analysts with production-like datasets for testing and analytics without exposing real PII. They need: consistent tokenization (same customer_id always maps to the same token for joins across tables), format preservation (masked credit card numbers should still look like credit card numbers for application testing), reversible de-identification for authorized compliance staff, and different masking policies for different user groups (analysts see masked data, compliance sees real data).
questions.questionText: Which GCP service provides consistent, format-preserving, reversible data masking with role-based policies?

choices.text: Application-level masking in the BI tool before displaying to users
Custom masking functions in BigQuery UDFs applied at query time
ETL pipeline creating separate masked datasets for each user group

BigQuery dynamic data masking with policy tags — different masking rules per policy tag, format-preserving options, and IAM-controlled visibility (fine-grained readers see unmasked data, regular users see masked data)

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: BigQuery dynamic data masking applies masking rules at query time based on the user's IAM role — same table, different visibility per user group.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: BigQuery dynamic data masking uses policy tags attached to columns. Masking rules define how data appears to different user groups: SHA256 hash (consistent tokenization — same input = same output, enabling joins), format-preserving masking (credit card appears as 4XXX-XXXX-XXXX-1234), or full nullification. IAM fine-grained reader roles control who sees unmasked data: compliance staff with the 'masked reader' role see original values (reversible access), regular analysts see the masked version. No data duplication, no separate datasets — single source of truth with visibility determined by user identity at query time.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Policy tag masking rules: DEFAULT (null), SHA256 (consistent hash), email masking (user@domain.com → u***@domain.com), and custom SQL expressions.
  • Format-preserving: custom masking rules can use SQL expressions like CONCAT(LEFT(card, 4), '-XXXX-XXXX-', RIGHT(card, 4)).
  • Consistent tokenization: SHA256 produces the same hash for the same input — customer_id joins work across masked tables.
  • Fine-grained reader: bigquery.dataPolicyUnmaskedReader role on specific policy tags reveals unmasked data — compliance team gets this role.

questions.title: Capacity Planning for BigQuery
questions.scenario: A company is planning their BigQuery architecture for the next year. Expected growth: data volume from 100TB to 500TB, query volume from 10,000 to 50,000 queries per day, concurrent users from 50 to 200, and they are adding 3 new real-time dashboards requiring sub-5-second response. They need to choose between on-demand pricing and editions (slot-based), and size their BI Engine reservation appropriately.
questions.questionText: Which capacity planning approach optimizes cost for the projected growth?

choices.text: Enterprise edition with baseline slots sized to handle average daily load, autoscaling for peak periods, BI Engine reservation sized to the total active working set of the 3 real-time dashboards, and monitoring to right-size quarterly
Stay on on-demand pricing and accept cost growth proportional to query volume
Purchase maximum possible slots upfront with annual commitment for the largest discount
Standard edition with no baseline and maximum autoscaling only

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Baseline slots for predictable load (cheapest) + autoscaling for peaks + BI Engine for sub-5s dashboards = cost-optimized capacity plan.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Enterprise edition provides the features needed (materialized views, BI Engine, security features). Baseline slots sized at the average daily slot consumption (calculated from current workload metrics) provide committed-rate pricing for predictable load. Autoscaling handles the variance — peak periods (50,000 queries during business hours) scale up automatically without over-provisioning for off-peak. BI Engine reservation sized to cache the working set of the 3 real-time dashboards ensures sub-5-second response without consuming query slots. Quarterly right-sizing reviews adjust baseline as growth materializes — avoiding both over-commitment and under-provisioning.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Capacity planning formula: analyze INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS to calculate average and p95 slot consumption over the past 30 days.
  • BI Engine sizing: total bytes of tables/MVs used by real-time dashboards — typically 1-50GB for most dashboard scenarios.
  • Enterprise edition: annual commitment for baseline slots provides ~60% discount vs. on-demand equivalent.
  • Monitoring: INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS_BY_ORGANIZATION view tracks slot utilization, queue times, and query failures for right-sizing decisions.

questions.title: Multi-Source Data Integration
questions.scenario: A company needs to integrate data from: Salesforce (CRM, 100 objects, incremental sync needed), SAP (ERP, 50 tables via OData), Google Analytics 4 (event data, 1B events/month), and internal REST APIs (5 services, real-time). All data must land in BigQuery for unified analytics. Each source has different authentication methods, rate limits, and data formats. The team wants managed connectors where possible to minimize custom development.
questions.questionText: Which combination of GCP ingestion services handles all four sources with minimal custom code?

choices.text: Custom Dataflow pipelines with source-specific I/O connectors for all four sources
AppSheet connected to each source feeding data into BigQuery via Sheets
Data Fusion for all four sources using visual connectors

BigQuery Data Transfer Service for Salesforce and GA4 (managed connectors with scheduling), Datastream for SAP (via HANA/S4 CDC or OData replication), and Pub/Sub with Cloud Functions for internal REST API real-time events

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Use managed connectors where they exist (BQ DTS for Salesforce/GA4, Datastream for databases) and lightweight serverless for real-time APIs.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: BigQuery Data Transfer Service provides managed, scheduled connectors for SaaS applications: Salesforce connector handles incremental sync of 100 objects with automatic schema mapping, and GA4 connector exports event data to BigQuery daily (a native Google integration). Datastream provides managed CDC/replication from SAP (connecting via OData or direct database replication for supported databases). For internal REST APIs requiring real-time integration, services push events to Pub/Sub topics, and Cloud Functions (or Dataflow) transform and load to BigQuery. This maximizes managed services (minimal code) while handling each source's specific protocol.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• BQ DTS Salesforce: automatic schema detection, incremental sync using Salesforce's Bulk API 2.0, handles API rate limits.
  • GA4 BigQuery export: native integration — enable in GA4 settings, data appears in BigQuery dataset automatically.
  • Datastream SAP: connects via SAP connectors or source database (HANA) for continuous replication to BigQuery.
  • Pub/Sub + Functions pattern: push-based (REST APIs push to Pub/Sub endpoint), serverless (no always-on compute), auto-scaling.

questions.title: Choosing Storage for Analytics Workloads
questions.scenario: A company evaluates storage options for three different analytics workloads: (1) a data warehouse for SQL analytics with 200 concurrent users and complex joins, (2) a machine learning feature store needing sub-10ms point lookups at 100K QPS, and (3) a data lake for unstructured data (images, PDFs, logs) that Spark and Dataflow jobs process in batch. Each has different performance, cost, and access pattern requirements.
questions.questionText: Which storage technology is optimal for each of the three workloads?

choices.text: BigQuery for all three workloads as a unified platform
Cloud SQL for analytics, Memorystore for features, and Cloud Storage for data lake

BigQuery for SQL analytics (columnar, massively parallel, SQL-native), Bigtable for ML feature store (sub-10ms point lookups at 100K+ QPS), Cloud Storage for data lake (unstructured, cost-effective, GCS connector for Spark/Dataflow)
Spanner for all three to get the benefits of strong consistency everywhere

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Match each workload to the storage optimized for its access pattern: columnar analytics (BigQuery), key-value lookups (Bigtable), object store (GCS).

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: BigQuery: purpose-built for SQL analytics with columnar storage, massively parallel execution, and support for 200+ concurrent users with complex joins — the gold standard for data warehouse workloads. Bigtable: designed for sub-10ms single-row lookups at extreme throughput (100K+ QPS scales linearly with nodes) — perfect for ML feature serving where the access pattern is "get features for user X instantly." Cloud Storage: object store for unstructured data at the lowest cost, with native connectors for Spark (GCS connector) and Dataflow (TextIO, FileIO) for batch processing. Each storage is optimized for its workload's specific access pattern.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• BigQuery: $6.25/TB queried (on-demand) or slot-based; columnar compression reduces actual storage; decoupled compute/storage.
  • Bigtable: $0.65/node/hour + $0.026/GB/month; each node handles 10K+ reads/second at single-digit ms latency.
  • Cloud Storage: $0.020/GB/month (Standard); no compute charges — processing via Dataproc/Dataflow only when jobs run.
  • Anti-patterns: BigQuery for point lookups (too slow), Bigtable for complex joins (no SQL), GCS for interactive queries (no compute engine).

questions.title: Connected Sheets for Business Users
questions.scenario: A finance team of 20 analysts currently exports BigQuery data to Google Sheets for analysis (pivot tables, charts, what-if scenarios). Problems: exports are limited to 10 million cells, data becomes stale immediately after export, and each analyst maintains their own copy. They need to work with billions of rows in a spreadsheet-like interface, always see fresh data, and collaborate on the same analysis without data duplication.
questions.questionText: Which feature connects business users' spreadsheet workflows directly to BigQuery at scale?

choices.text: Scheduled data exports from BigQuery to Sheets on a timer

Connected Sheets — Google Sheets directly querying BigQuery data with pivot tables, charts, and calculated columns on billions of rows without data extraction, always showing live data, and enabling real-time collaboration
Looker embedded analytics within Sheets
BigQuery BI Engine connected to a custom web-based spreadsheet application

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Connected Sheets provides a native Sheets interface that queries BigQuery in real-time — no export needed, no cell limits on the underlying data.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Connected Sheets is a Google Sheets feature that creates a live connection to BigQuery tables. Analysts work in the familiar Sheets interface — creating pivot tables, charts, and formulas — but the underlying data stays in BigQuery (no 10M cell limit, data is always fresh). When an analyst creates a pivot table on a billion-row BigQuery table, Sheets sends the aggregation query to BigQuery and displays only the result. Multiple analysts collaborate on the same Sheet with the same live connection — no data duplication. BigQuery IAM controls who can access which datasets, and query costs are attributed to the user's project.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Connected Sheets queries BigQuery on interaction — pivot table changes generate new BigQuery queries in real-time.
  • No data extraction: underlying billions of rows never leave BigQuery; only aggregated results appear in Sheets.
  • Calculated columns: Sheets formulas translated to BigQuery SQL — computed at BigQuery scale, not in the browser.
  • Collaboration: multiple users on the same Connected Sheet see the same live data — changes propagate in real-time like normal Sheets.

questions.title: Organization-Wide Data Governance
questions.scenario: A multinational corporation with 100 GCP projects across 10 business units needs organization-wide data governance. Requirements: prevent any project from storing data outside approved regions (EU data in europe-*, US data in us-*), enforce encryption with CMEK on all BigQuery datasets, require all Cloud Storage buckets to have uniform bucket-level access (no ACLs), and ensure no public access to any storage resources. These must be enforced automatically — human compliance checks are insufficient.
questions.questionText: Which GCP mechanism provides automated, organization-wide enforcement of these governance policies?

choices.text: Security Command Center with manual remediation of violations
Custom scripts running daily to check and remediate non-compliant resources

Organization Policies — constraints applied at the organization or folder level: resource location restriction (allowed regions), require CMEK for BigQuery, enforce uniform bucket-level access, and disable public access on all storage resources — automatically enforced on all projects without project-level configuration
IAM deny policies preventing users from creating resources in non-compliant configurations

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Organization Policies provide preventive controls that automatically enforce rules across all projects — resources that violate the policy cannot be created.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Organization Policy Service defines constraints inherited by all projects: gcp.resourceLocations restricts resource creation to allowed regions (preventing EU data in US regions), constraints/gcp.detailedAuditLoggingMode and CMEK constraints require encryption, storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess enforces uniform access (no legacy ACLs), and storage.publicAccessPrevention blocks any public access configuration. These are preventive — a user attempting to create a non-compliant resource receives an error immediately. Policies set at the organization or folder level are inherited by all child projects automatically — no per-project configuration needed. New projects are immediately compliant.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Organization Policies are preventive (block creation) vs. SCC/Config (detective — find after creation). Preventive is stronger for compliance.
  • Resource location constraint: supports allow-list (only these regions) or deny-list (not these regions) — applied to all resource types.
  • Policy inheritance: Org → Folder → Project — child policies can be more restrictive but not less restrictive than parent.
  • Custom organization policies (preview): write custom rules using CEL (Common Expression Language) for constraints not covered by built-in policies.
